title: Analyze an Op-Amp Amplifier
prompt: You're handed a non-inverting op-amp stage: a signal into the + input, a feedback resistor Rf from the output to the - input, and a resistor Rin from that - input to ground. Walk me through how you analyze it — the assumptions you make, how you get the closed-loop gain and input/output impedance, and how bandwidth and slew rate limit what this stage can actually do. Pick some component values and work a real number.
blurb: Spoken station — analyze a non-inverting op-amp stage: ideal-op-amp assumptions, closed-loop gain, impedance, gain-bandwidth and slew-rate limits, and real non-idealities.

rubric.label: Ideal-op-amp assumptions
rubric.description: States and justifies the idealizations used to analyze the stage: the virtual short (V+ = V-) from high open-loop gain plus negative feedback, negligible input bias current (infinite input impedance), and zero output impedance; is clear these are approximations.

rubric.label: Closed-loop gain derivation
rubric.description: Derives the non-inverting closed-loop gain 1 + Rf/Rin from the virtual short and the feedback divider, rather than reciting it; can contrast with the inverting configuration (-Rf/Rin) and explain the feedback-divider β = Rin/(Rin+Rf).

rubric.label: Input & output impedance
rubric.description: Explains that the non-inverting topology presents a very high input impedance (loop-gain-boosted) and low output impedance, why that makes it a good buffer/first stage, and how feedback reduces output impedance by the loop gain.

rubric.label: Gain-bandwidth & bandwidth
rubric.description: Uses the gain-bandwidth product (GBW ≈ constant for a dominant-pole op-amp) to compute closed-loop bandwidth = GBW / closed-loop gain, and explains the gain-bandwidth tradeoff.

rubric.label: Slew rate & non-idealities
rubric.description: Distinguishes small-signal bandwidth from large-signal slew-rate limiting (full-power bandwidth), and raises real non-idealities: input offset voltage, bias/offset currents, finite open-loop gain, output saturation near the rails, and noise.

rubric.label: Worked numeric example
rubric.description: Carries a concrete example end to end: picks resistor values, computes the gain, then computes the resulting bandwidth from a stated GBW (and ideally sanity-checks the slew-rate limit), with correct units.

rubric.label: Communication & structure
rubric.description: Lays out the analysis in an organized way, thinks aloud, defines symbols, and sanity-checks results rather than just asserting formulas.

reference.scenario: A candidate is asked to analyze a non-inverting op-amp amplifier stage. The station tests whether they can reason from ideal-op-amp assumptions to closed-loop behavior — gain, input/output impedance — and then layer in the real limits that matter in practice: finite gain-bandwidth product, slew rate, offset, and the supply rails. A strong candidate derives results rather than reciting them, works a concrete numeric example, and knows when the ideal model breaks down. This is an educational reasoning exercise, not a substitute for real design verification, SPICE simulation, or datasheet sign-off.
model_points: Ideal-op-amp model: infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance (no input current), zero output impedance, infinite bandwidth — used as a first approximation and refined later.
Virtual short: with negative feedback and huge open-loop gain, the op-amp drives V- to equal V+, so the inverting input tracks the input signal even though no current flows into either input.

Closed-loop gain of the non-inverting stage: the feedback network Rf/Rin divides the output back to V-; setting V- = Vin gives Vout/Vin = 1 + Rf/Rin (the feedback factor β = Rin/(Rin+Rf), and closed-loop gain ≈ 1/β for large loop gain).

Input impedance is very high (signal drives the + input directly, boosted by the loop gain), output impedance is low (Zout,closed ≈ Zout,open / loop gain), making the stage a good buffer or front end; a unity-gain follower is the Rf=0 / Rin=∞ limit.

Gain-bandwidth product (GBW): for a dominant-pole (single-pole compensated) op-amp the product of closed-loop gain and bandwidth is roughly constant, so closed-loop bandwidth f_3dB ≈ GBW / closed-loop gain — the fundamental gain-vs-speed tradeoff.

Slew rate is a separate large-signal limit (dV/dt max, set by internal current charging the compensation capacitor); full-power bandwidth f_FP = SR / (2·π·Vpeak). Small-signal bandwidth and slew-limited full-power bandwidth are different ceilings — the lower one governs.
Finite open-loop gain A causes a small gain error: actual gain = ideal / (1 + 1/(Aβ)); as A rolls off with frequency the loop gain shrinks and gain error grows.

DC non-idealities: input offset voltage (amplified by the noise gain 1 + Rf/Rin and appearing as an output DC error), input bias and offset currents through the resistors (mitigate with a balancing resistor and by keeping resistances moderate), and input-referred noise.

Output can only swing within the supply rails (or closer with a rail-to-rail part); clipping/saturation occurs when gain×input exceeds the available swing, so gain and signal amplitude must fit the rails.

Worked example: Rin = 1 kΩ, Rf = 9 kΩ → gain = 1 + 9k/1k = 10 (20 dB). With a GBW of 10 MHz, closed-loop bandwidth ≈ 10 MHz / 10 = 1 MHz. Check slew: for a 1 Vpeak output and SR = 5 V/µs, full-power bandwidth = 5e6 / (2π·1) ≈ 0.8 MHz, so a 1 V, 1 MHz sine would be slightly slew-limited — the slew limit, not the small-signal bandwidth, dominates for large signals.

probes.trigger: candidate recites 1 + Rf/Rin without justifying it
probes.question: Where does that formula come from? Walk me through it starting from what the two inputs do.

probes.trigger: candidate treats bandwidth as fixed regardless of gain
probes.question: If you doubled the closed-loop gain, what happens to the bandwidth, and why?

probes.trigger: candidate conflates bandwidth with slew rate
probes.question: Your small-signal bandwidth says 1 MHz. Would a 5-volt-peak square-ish signal at that frequency actually come through cleanly? What else limits you?

probes.trigger: candidate assumes the op-amp is perfectly ideal
probes.question: This is a real part with finite gain and some input offset. Where does the ideal model start to lie to you?
You've got gain of 100 and a 50 mV DC offset at the input on a ±5 V supply. Any problem?
Pick real resistor values and a GBW and tell me the actual gain and bandwidth you'd get.

red_flags: Reciting gain = 1 + Rf/Rin (or the inverting -Rf/Rin) with no derivation and mixing up which configuration is which.
Claiming current flows into the ideal op-amp inputs, or not understanding the virtual short requires negative feedback.
Treating bandwidth as independent of gain / not knowing the gain-bandwidth product tradeoff.
Confusing slew-rate (large-signal) limiting with small-signal bandwidth, or ignoring slew entirely.
Ignoring the supply rails / output saturation and offset amplification (noise gain).
Assuming infinite open-loop gain gives zero gain error at all frequencies.
Getting units or orders of magnitude wrong in the worked example (e.g., Hz vs MHz).
No numeric example at all despite being asked.
follow_ups: Redo this as an inverting amplifier — how do the gain, input impedance, and the virtual-ground node change?
Your open-loop gain rolls off at -20 dB/decade above a low pole. How does that shape the closed-loop response and stability?
How would input offset voltage and bias current show up at the output, and how would you minimize their effect?
When would you add a capacitor across Rf, and what does it do to the frequency response?
How do you check this stage is stable — what do phase margin and the feedback factor have to do with it?
reference.exemplar_answer: I'd start from the ideal-op-amp assumptions and refine from there. Ideally the op-amp has infinite open-loop gain, no input current, and zero output impedance. Because there's negative feedback and huge open-loop gain, the op-amp drives its inverting input to match the non-inverting input — the virtual short — so V- equals Vin, while essentially no current flows into either input. The feedback network is just Rf and Rin forming a divider from the output: V- = Vout·Rin/(Rin+Rf). Setting that equal to Vin gives Vout/Vin = 1 + Rf/Rin. So if I pick Rin = 1 kΩ and Rf = 9 kΩ, the closed-loop gain is 10, or 20 dB. Because the signal drives the + input directly, the input impedance is very high, and negative feedback drives the output impedance down by the loop gain, so this makes a good buffered front end. For speed I use the gain-bandwidth product: for a dominant-pole op-amp, gain times bandwidth is roughly constant, so with a 10 MHz GBW my closed-loop bandwidth is about 10 MHz divided by the gain of 10, which is 1 MHz — that's the gain-versus-speed tradeoff. But small-signal bandwidth isn't the whole story: slew rate is a separate large-signal limit. If the part slews at 5 V/µs, the full-power bandwidth for a 1-volt-peak output is SR over 2π·Vpeak, about 0.8 MHz, so a large signal near 1 MHz would actually start to slew-limit before the small-signal bandwidth bites — the lower ceiling wins. Then the real non-idealities: finite open-loop gain gives a small gain error that grows as the gain rolls off; input offset voltage gets amplified by the noise gain of 1 + Rf/Rin and shows up as a DC output error; bias currents through the resistors add offset, which I'd manage with a balancing resistor and moderate resistor values; and the output can only swing within the rails, so I keep gain times signal inside the supply range to avoid clipping. I'd confirm the final design in simulation and against the datasheet.

interviewer_notes: Mid-level analog circuits station on a non-inverting op-amp stage. Reward a candidate who derives the closed-loop gain from the virtual short and the feedback divider rather than reciting 1 + Rf/Rin, and who cleanly separates the three limits that matter: small-signal bandwidth via the gain-bandwidth product, large-signal slew-rate limiting, and the supply rails. Push them to pick real numbers and carry a worked example through gain and bandwidth; a strong answer sanity-checks the slew limit too. Feed non-idealities (offset, finite gain, a saturating output) to see if they know when the ideal model breaks. Do not require exact datasheet parameters or SPICE precision — reward correct method, correct orders of magnitude, and clear reasoning. Common failure modes to flag: confusing inverting vs non-inverting, thinking bandwidth is independent of gain, and conflating slew rate with bandwidth.
